world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Si accentano graficamente solo le parole che hanno piú di una vocale grafica, eccetto quelle il cui l'accento d'intensità sillabica cade sulla penultima vocale. Esempi di applicazione della regola: mi, ti, si, la, lu, li (una sola vocale, nessun accento) / cosa, ommu (due vocali, accento ritmico implicito sulla penultima) / zurradda, abia, cuccummiau (piú di due vocali, accento ritmico implicito sulla penultima) / piú (o più), parchí (o parchì), farà, aió (accento esplicito sull'ultima) / fèmmina, pazènzia, pégura, sciòbaru, àgliu, faràbami (accento esplicito sulla terzultima) / tinàgliuru, fazarísthiani (accento esplicito sulla quartultima).
new_statements.translation: Only words with more than one written vowel are given a graphic accent, except those in which the syllabic intensity stress falls on the penultimate vowel. Examples of the rule: mi, ti, si, la, lu, li (one vowel, no accent) / cosa, ommu (two vowels, rhythmic stress implicit on the penult) / zurradda, abia, cuccummiau (more than two vowels, rhythmic stress implicit on the penult) / piú, parchí, farà, aió (explicit stress on the last) / fèmmina, pazènzia, pégura, sciòbaru, àgliu, faràbami (explicit stress on the antepenult) / tinàgliuru, fazarísthiani (explicit stress on the fourth-from-last).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress ('accento d'intensità sillabica', which the source equates with 'accento di parola / tonico / ritmico', p. 20) is fixed per lexical item, as in Italian and Corsican. The unmarked and majority position is the penultimate syllable (the orthography leaves it unmarked); final stress is common and systematic in a whole class (all infinitives farà, abé, finí, bí, dà; also caffè, aió, parchí, piú) and is the only obligatory graphic accent; antepenultimate stress occurs in many nouns/adjectives and verb forms (fèmmina, pégura, àgliu, faràbami), and pre-antepenultimate stress in verb forms with enclitics (tinàgliuru, fazarísthiani). Stress is contrastive: farà /faˈra/ 'to go down' vs fara /ˈfara/ '(s)he goes down' (p. 20).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the phrase-level IPA transcriptions in § 3.3 mark secondary stresses on proclitic groups (e.g. par imparà [ˌpaˑɾimpaˈɾa], pa' fribàggiu [ˌpaffɾiˈβaˑʤˑʤu], pp. 37-38).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic clitics mi, ti, si, la, lu, li carry no stress; pronominal/adverbial enclitic particles are stressless and stress stays on the verb, yielding antepenult/pre-antepenult stress in verb+clitic forms (§ 3.3, § 4.10); in the 'amplified' 1st-conjugation verbs the stressed infix appears in forms stressed on the antepenult/fourth-from-last, while 1st/2nd plural forms are stressed on the penult (§ 4.10.5, p. 65). Homographs distinguished by stress and by mid-vowel timbre are listed (pp. 9-10, 23).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms), explicitly 'accento di parola'; the document is a normative orthography with a phonetics/phonology outline covering the Turritano varieties of Sassari, Porto Torres, Sorso and Stintino (Castelsardo/castellanese excluded). The statement is framed as a rule for graphic accentuation, from which the stress positions are read off; no frequency counts are given.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2022 standard describes 'turritano/sassarese' as spoken in Sassari, Porto Torres, Sorso and Stintino (= Glottolog sass1235 Sassarese Sardinian); it explicitly excludes castellanese (Castelsardo). Glottolog's Jäggli 1959 (Sennori) describes a north-Logudorese Sardinian dialect, not Sassarese, and should not be used for this key.

sources.note: Neither article states where stress falls; the Italian article's bibliography and its pointer to the 2022 standard (archived comune.sassari.it PDFs) led to the sources above.

sources.citation: Guarnerio, Pier Enea. 1896-98. I dialetti odierni di Sassari, della Gallura e della Corsica (continuazione e fine). Archivio Glottologico Italiano XIV, 131-200, 385-422.
sources.note: Historical phonology only. Paragraph 'Accento' (nm. 194, p. 186) lists a handful of words whose stress differs from the Latin etymon (sass. pittorra < PECTORA 'petto'; gall. kuppiuli vs sass. kuppiglu; gall. ambula < AMPULLA) plus analogical shifts in the conjugation (nm. 219, 231: retracted stress in 1st/2nd pl. of subjunctive/imperfect); no general statement of where stress falls.

sources.citation: Guarnerio, Pier Enea. 1892-94. I dialetti odierni di Sassari, della Gallura e della Corsica. Archivio Glottologico Italiano XIII, 125-140.
sources.note: Section 'Vocali toniche' treats reflexes of stressed Latin vowels; mentions proparoxytones (pessigu, plbara) and non-rhizotonic forms incidentally; no stress-placement rule.

sources.citation: Toso, Fiorenzo. 2018. Un profilo del sassarese. In Krefeld, Thomas & Bauer, Roland (eds.), Lo spazio comunicativo dell'Italia e delle varietà italiane (Korpus im Text 7). LMU München.
sources.note: § 4 'Caratteri del sassarese': among the Corsican-type traits shared with Gallurese against Logudorese it lists 'la significativa presenza dell'ossitonia (carà 'calare', cancarà 'intirizzire')'; 7 stressed vowels reduced to 3 unstressed; no general stress rule.
